Although systematic limitations remain the dominant source of uncertainty for the upcoming era of CMB cosmology, these complexities are difficult to quantify because of a scarcity of high-fidelity simulations alongside pure prototype tests. To address this, we introduce `scn`, a Python/c++ toolkit capable of rapidly generating the CMB and foreground signals for arbitrary pixelated sky maps as well as applying a broad spectrum of instrumental artifacts to mimic real-world data. By offering a swift replacement for intricate physical models, `scn` enables the inversion-based analysis that is essential for placing accurate limits on systematic effects. When paired with full-simulation pipelines that incorporate both the instrument's beam and integration times as well as integration paths, `scn` allows researchers to move toward fully instrument-specific treatments of these systematic issues. Ultimately, we demonstrate that incorporating sky map simulations significantly exceeds simplified approaches in terms of benefit, providing a far more significant reduction in systematic uncertainty than the benefits derived from map alone would suggest in practical applications. Therefore, `scn` emerges as an invaluable asset for exploring the complexities inherent in next-generation CMB experiments.

relies heavily on negation, yet despite its universal presence across all languages, it remains a significant obstacle for current natural language understanding systems. To advance the creation of models capable of handling negated speech effectively, we introduce **CONDAQA**, an English reading comprehension resource explicitly focused on the capability to discern implied information within statements. Distinctive features include an examination of diverse pragmatic strategies used for negation and a comprehensive catalog of 27,000 dialogue examples spanning 189 categories of negated inquiries. Our analysis reveals that resolving these questions requires a combination of detecting the point of negation and applying this insight to access knowledge/subtext not directly present in the text itself to answer user queries. To push current model boundaries, we organized diverse challenge sets composed specifically of "short-circuiting" examples—instances where simple keywords trigger incorrect responses—that force state-of-the-art architectures to demonstrate they can correctly answer questions with their own external memory and reasoning abilities. Ultimately, our work provides detailed annotation guidelines highlighting key differences in how various forms of negated questioning are expressed in natural dialogue, alongside extensive evaluation results indicating that even advanced state-of-the-art models struggle significantly with this specific subset of tasks compared to human standards. Both sources code and annotation data can be accessed here: https://condqa.github.io/.

These attacks covertly insert hidden functionalities into neural networks that activate only when specific trigger patterns appear in the input. Most existing research utilizes manual methods to generate these triggers, a process that is inherently constrained and difficult to perfect. Recently, researchers demonstrated a significant breakthrough with autonomous, map-free techniques for generating replacement filters that serve as effective backdoor mechanisms. Nonetheless, current collaborative learning protocols utilizing these backdoors remain exclusively dependent on the presence of a compromised model update. We propose Neural Computation Backdoor (NCB), an innovative approach that injects a backdoor directly into the training process of a model being updated within a cloud setting, without needing any prior alteration to the global model itself. Our results indicate that NCB is difficult to detect and robust against various input distributions yet remain somewhat susceptible to adversarial inputs. Additionally, we highlight a defense mechanism built upon an analysis of feature redundancy to effectively neutralize the NCB attack.

We formalize the problem within the Functional Encryption (FE) framework, specifically targeting Machine Learning Inference (FE-MI). In this setting, the encrypted input contains unrestricted data, while the decoder can utilize a model $f$ to derive the result $x \mapsto f(x)$ only when it aligns with a predetermined function $z$. We establish two distinct definitions for FE-MI, offering either one level of granularity or granular control over which aspects of the model are exposed. Recognizing that existing FE designs are ill-suited for practical application, our construction leverages standard, reliable FE templates. However, requiring the model $f$ to be linear is a significant limitation, effectively precluding many popular models; therefore, our approach relaxes linearity requirements by enforcing linearity on just the encryption-related component. We detail how to adapt $f$ from its raw form to a decomposed structure composed of classical, linear FE-compatible components, ensuring secure inference without restrictive assumptions on $f$. We also present an alternative, alternative construction that supports selective (pre-agreed) data access, extending the feasibility of FE-MI to advanced scenarios. We validate our approach by implementing FE-driven support vector regression, demonstrating that our method successfully reduces overhead compared to generic, state-of-the-art FE protocols when applied to real-world data sets.
